intro: The Concertgebouw strings under Willem Mengelberg, who knew Mahler and championed his music, play the Adagietto (Sehr langsam), the fourth movement of Mahler’s Symphony No. 5. The recording was made in Amsterdam in 1926. The strings slide between notes together, and the tempo is flexible.

sections.label: A · Harp and strings, Sehr langsam
sections.mNote: The violin melody leans and moves freely.

sections.label: B · Middle section, strings
sections.mNote: Melody on the G string; harmony moves towards G♭ major.

sections.label: A′ · Opening theme returns, slower
sections.mNote: The harp returns beneath the lengthened violin phrase.

sections.label: A″ · High violins, rising cellos
sections.mNote: The final phrase broadens to its highest point.

sections.label: Coda · Strings in F major
sections.mNote: The harp stops before the last held chord.

cues.title: First violin entry, Mengelberg
cues.text: Harp and low strings play before the first violins enter. Mengelberg places their pickup early in the bar, and the phrase then broadens. The tempo changes slightly within the long melodic line.
cues.evidence: Jonathan Manton describes the anticipatory opening pickup and flexible pulse in this recording: https://guides.library.yale.edu/c.php?g=525668&p=4452898 . Opening instrumentation: Peters score, plate 9015, p. 178.

cues.title: String portamento
cues.text: The strings slide audibly between some notes, moving together as a section. Mengelberg makes these portamento slides part of the phrase, along with its pauses and abrupt changes of tempo.
cues.evidence: Manton’s discussion of this recording identifies coordinated string portamento and abrupt local tempo changes: https://guides.library.yale.edu/c.php?g=525668&p=4452898 . This note describes the performance’s string phrasing across the passage.

cues.title: Mengelberg and Mahler, Krefeld, 1902
cues.text: At Krefeld in 1902 Mengelberg heard Mahler conduct the première of his Third Symphony, and he invited him to Amsterdam the following year. The Concertgebouw became one of Mahler’s strongest homes. Mengelberg went on conducting the music after the composer’s death.
cues.evidence: Manton’s account of Mengelberg’s encounter with Mahler in Krefeld, the 1903 Amsterdam invitation and his later advocacy: https://guides.library.yale.edu/c.php?g=525668&p=4452898

cues.title: Columbia L 1798, Amsterdam, 1926
cues.text: The Adagietto filled both sides of Columbia L 1798, recorded in the Concertgebouw in May 1926 (matrices WAX 1548 and 1549). This transfer from the original 78 rpm disc joins the two sides in a single file.
cues.evidence: Internet Archive item “Willem Mengelberg, Concertgebouw Orch. Amsterdam, Columbia L 1798” gives the label number, matrices, place and date of recording and the transfer from the original 78: https://archive.org/details/willem-mengelberg-cgo-col-l-1798-wax-1548-9-1926

cues.title: Fliessender section, strings alone
cues.text: At Fliessender, the harp stops and the violins play a melody on the G string, marked mit Wärme. The harmony moves towards G♭ major. The strings play most of this middle section alone, with one brief return of harp arpeggios in bars 45–48.
cues.evidence: Peters full score, plate 9015, p. 180: Fliessender, G-Saite, mit Wärme and grosser Ton; harp returns in bars 45–48 before the G♭-major passage. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/04/IMSLP13083-Mahler-Symphony_No.5_IV.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Reprise of the first melody
cues.text: The harp triplets return beneath the held strings, and the first melody begins again. Mengelberg takes this reprise more slowly than the opening. Its long notes extend across the bar while the harp plays shorter notes beneath them.
cues.evidence: Manton identifies the slower return in this recording: https://guides.library.yale.edu/c.php?g=525668&p=4452898 . Harp re-entry and Tempo I: Peters score, p. 181.

cues.title: Adagietto performance timings
cues.text: Mahler and Mengelberg played the Adagietto in about seven minutes. Mengelberg’s 1926 disc lasts seven minutes seventeen seconds. Modern performances often take ten minutes or more.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s movement page gives about seven minutes for Mahler and Mengelberg and up to nearly twelve for modern recordings: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-movement-4-adagietto-sehr-langsam/ . The Internet Archive transfer runs 7:17: https://archive.org/details/willem-mengelberg-cgo-col-l-1798-wax-1548-9-1926

cues.title: Final crescendo, violins
cues.text: The violins climb over rising cellos and harp arpeggios. Mahler marks the strings breiter Strich, viel Bogen wechseln and viel Ton, and the basses play arco beneath them. The phrase then descends.
cues.evidence: Peters score, p. 182, final crescendo: breiter Strich, viel Bogen wechseln, viel Ton and arco basses.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final chord and fermata
cues.text: The harp rests. Strings descend into the last F major chord and hold it under a long fermata. In the complete symphony, Mahler marked the Rondo-Finale to begin without a break.
cues.evidence: Peters score, p. 182, final system: harp rests, F-major string ending, long fermatas and attacca Rondo-Finale.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor.
